look_here_first: COMMON REED (Phragmites): a tall rhizomatous wetland GRASS with jointed stems, long blades, and enormous silky branched plumes. But DO NOT equate species name with invasive: North American native subsp. americanus, Eurasian introduced lineage (often subsp. australis), and Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri/cryptogenic lineage all occur in the broader Texas region. Inspect real SHEATH, STEM, LIGULE and ripe GLUMES before assigning lineage; Texas state-level native presence does not prove Hays County occurrence.

best_field_traits: Strong reed-like perennial: upright tall jointed culms, broad linear leaves, underground rhizomes, feathery panicles, and multi-flowered spikelets with silky rachilla hairs
Species-level identification: inspect a true multi-flowered spikelet with long silky rachilla hairs, not a single tuft or simply 'cane'

Native-lineage americanus often has shiny smooth red-brown exposed late-season stems, older sheaths readily loose/caducous, generally ligules 1.0–1.7 mm; long glumes often lower 3–6.5 and upper 5.5–11 mm
Introduced Eurasian lineage often has duller/ridged stems and persistent tightly clasping leaf sheaths, ligules 0.4–0.9 mm, lower glumes 2.5–5.0 and upper 4.5–7.5 mm; these measurements overlap

Gulf Coast berlandieri lineage is additional concern in Texas/southern U.S.; its historical origin and taxonomy are treated differently by USGS and Kew; morphology/genetics and provenance may be required
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole reed colony, flowering panicle and wetland habitat with scale; compare stand structure but do not decide native from density
SAME LIVE culm near mid-stem: shiny or ridged exposed internode with node, aging leaf sheath wrapped or gaping, and true collar
5–10 intact ligules measured next to 1-mm rule under 10–20×; photo identifies actual blade/sheath junction and hair fringe
Five ripe matched lower and upper glumes detached with accurate 1-mm ruler; annotate each glume separately
Silky spikelet/rachilla hairs, fertile lemma and flowering head macros; compare Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea
Document locality and collect voucher or DNA/haplotype evidence for disputed Gulf / native / Eurasian lineages BEFORE treatment
crew_field_check: FIRST: is it the species common reed? Look for large silky feathery panicles and true reed leaf/sheath with multi-flowered spikelets; compare Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea.
NEXT: a species-level Phragmites ID is NOT an invasive designation. Texas has native americanus, introduced Eurasian and disputed-origin Gulf Coast berlandieri lineages.
On SAME mature culm, compare sheath detachment, smooth reddish glossy versus dull ridged exposed stem, and measure ligule (native often 1–1.7 mm, introduced often 0.4–0.9).
At 10–20× measure lower and upper ripe glumes (americanus generally longer; actual distributions overlap). Count 3–4 independent traits; winter photo and panicle colors alone do not suffice.
Photograph both flower and vegetative parts, season/locality, and consult a knowledgeable herbarium or genotype for ambiguous Gulf Coast or management-critical records.
Do not spray/mow as exotic solely on a big stand or seedhead: label Phragmites australis, lineage undetermined until actually verified.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Arundo donax (giant reed) has thicker bamboo-like canes, large leaf blades and structurally different plume/spikelets; Zizaniopsis miliacea (giant cutgrass) has a large but more open inflorescence and its leaf blades can cut skin. Within Phragmites, native American reed, introduced Eurasian reed and Gulf Coast reed cannot be reliably split by plume silhouette alone. Compare SHEATH persistence and stem texture + measured LIGULE and lower/upper GLUMES; verify uncertain Gulf Coast lineage with herbarium/genetic evidence.

CRITICAL: Phragmites australis includes native North American and invasive introduced lineages. items.why_it_matters: Arundo donax (giant reed) has bamboo-like robust stems, frequently wide leaves and different denser seedhead spikelets; Zizaniopsis miliacea (giant cutgrass) is another tall native wetland grass with a more open panicle and different spikelets. To distinguish Phragmites native vs introduced, compare multi-character sheath, leaf, culm and glume traits and ideally genetics/provenance; never a single seedhead.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Common reed — lineage is a SECOND diagnosis
steps: FIRST identify species, NOT lineage: tall wetland reed, jointed culms, broad leaves and branched silky flowering plume. Photo #1 teaches species habit only.

OPEN existing Harry Rose collar/ligule photograph (#2); locate its hair-fringed blade/sheath junction. This source is not Hays-vouchered or lineage confirmed. On a Texas specimen photograph 5–10 fresh actual ligules with 1-mm ruler; do not infer lineage from this photo.

OPEN existing Harry Rose annotated spikelet (#3) to learn where glumes, florets and rachilla occur. It cannot authenticate a native or exotic lineage; collect ripe intact same-culm spikelets and photograph separated upper/lower glumes at 1-mm scale.

CHECK multiple aged culms after midsummer: is each older leaf sheath naturally falling free or still firmly wrapped? Exposed internodes glossy reddish and smooth versus dull/ridged can SUPPORT a lineage hypothesis, but seasonal aging complicates comparison.

For typical non-Gulf populations, published ligule ranges trend native americanus ~1.0–1.7 mm versus introduced Eurasian ~0.4–0.9 mm; glumes also differ statistically and ranges overlap. Photograph and measure replicated parts, not one leaf.

TEXAS WARNING: Gulf Coast lineage (often called berlandieri) may resemble introduced Eurasian reed. A short ligule, persistent sheath or large monoculture does NOT resolve this third lineage; regional morphological keys may be unreliable.

For any proposed removal or planting, keep 'Phragmites australis — LINEAGE UNRESOLVED' until a specialist confirms several independent traits and, when needed, voucher/DNA haplotype. Never apply invasive management from silhouette or one photo.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Species ID first; lineage requires multiple independent characters. In Texas explicitly account for Gulf Coast lineage, whose morphology can overlap Eurasian introduced forms. Unresolved = no native/exotic decision.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: The three existing physically listed images illustrate whole reed, source-named ligule, and spikelet anatomy, NOT confirmed Texan lineage. No new lineage-specific macro or genetic evidence archived. Photo count and visible arrows are unchanged.
